1:
Keil alone lays down the law that the whole chapter turns on. Under the theocratic constitution Jehovah was the actual owner of the land he had given his people for an inheritance, so that they held only the usufruct of what fell to them by lot; the possessor could not part with the family portion at his own will, and it was to remain for ever in his family. From the account of how the advice was carried out, he adds, we learn that Naomi had instructed Ruth to ask Boaz to marry her as her redeemer — that is, to make a claim the law already recognised.

What Naomi meant by it is read three ways. Henry gives two motives and commends both: justice to the dead, that seed might be raised up to those that were gone and the family not made extinct; and gratitude to a daughter-in-law who had behaved dutifully. He notes that Naomi, having resolved on perpetual widowhood herself, was far from confining a young woman to it, since age must not make itself a standard to youth, and that she projected for her daughter what the daughter's modesty forbade her to project for herself. From the word rest he draws that a married state is, or should be, a state of rest to young people, wandering affections being then fixed — those are giddy indeed whom marriage does not compose — and that it is necessary to choose well, since otherwise it may prove the greatest uneasiness instead of a rest. Ellicott takes the same two motives and adds a third, that Naomi feared her own death would leave her young companion unprotected and friendless; and he presses the second clause as Henry does, that the object is Ruth's good and so it should be with every marriage, for the good and comfort and abiding peace not of the body only but of the soul. Gill keeps to the ground of the claim: Boaz was thought the next nearest kinsman, and so obliged by the law to marry her.

Whether the means were proper is the real question, and two of them raise it. Henry calls the course very extraordinary and admits it looks suspicious: if there was anything improper in it the fault must lie on Naomi, who put her daughter upon it and knew, or should have known, the laws and usages of Israel better than Ruth. Clarke goes further. Had Boaz not been a person of extraordinary piety, prudence and continence, he says, the experiment might have been fatal to Ruth; we cannot easily account for the transaction, and probably Naomi knew more than she revealed; it was dangerous, and should in no sense be imitated. Ellicott raises no difficulty at all.

The gesture itself gets three explanations. Ellicott renders it literally as lifting the clothes that lie on the feet, and reports that the custom still prevails of owners of crops sleeping on their threshing-floors with their clothes on but their feet covered by a mantle. Clarke makes it a marital usage, women in the East going to the bed of their lawful husbands, through modesty and in token of subjection, by the bed's foot, gently raising the clothes to creep under them. Wesley reduces it to a device for waking him. Around it the smaller details are agreed. Clarke describes the winnowing as letting a portion of the corn fall slowly from a broad thin vessel in the wind, the grain dropping by its own weight while the chaff is carried off, and explains the hour by the sea breeze that set in at evening; Wesley adds that the floor was covered overhead but open at the sides, the work usually ending in a feast. Gill and Clarke agree on the washing and the raiment, that she might appear clean and neat and be the better received.
5:
Ruth's compliance is defended two ways. Gill grounds it on her judgment of Naomi, of whose piety and prudence she had the highest opinion, being confident she would never advise what was contrary to religion and virtue. Ellicott grounds it on Ruth's own: her obedience is an intelligent obedience, since she knew in what relation Boaz stood to her family and what duties attached to it, so that she follows with a trust implicit but not blind, and, strong in conscious innocence, risks the obloquy that may attend her duty.

Henry alone treats what follows as a lesson in household management. When the servants winnowed, Boaz was with them and had his eye on them — not against their stealing his corn, for he had no reason to fear that, but against waste through carelessness, since masters may sustain great losses by servants who are heedless though honest. When there was more than ordinary work he gave them extraordinary entertainment and ate with them, it well becoming the rich and great to be both generous to and familiar with those employed under them. He went to bed in due time, so early that by midnight he had had his first sleep, all good husbands keeping good hours and not indulging themselves or their families in unseasonable mirth. And he lay at the corn-heap not because his heart was set on it, nor merely to guard it, but because it was too late to go home and he would be near his work next morning — showing besides that he was not nice in his lodging, but, like his father Jacob, a plain man who could on occasion make his bed in a barn.

Three of them repeat the Chaldee paraphrase, which adds that Boaz blessed the name of the Lord who had heard his prayer and taken the famine away. Gill and Clarke report it; Henry builds on it, inferring that Boaz went sober to bed with his heart in a good frame and not overcharged with surfeiting, and did not go to bed without prayer — which was well, since he had an unusual temptation before him and knew nothing of it. Gill adds that the eating and drinking was free but not to excess, innocent mirth having always been allowed in harvest, and explains the sleeping from the dress: Boaz lay on the straw with his clothes on, covering his feet with the lower part of his garment, since long garments served to sleep in by night as well as to cover by day, nor was it thought unworthy of persons of note to sleep so. Clarke supposes something more deliberate: since threshing-floors in the East are in the open air, the owner or a trusted man stayed in the fields till the grain was secured, keeping a tent at the place, and Boaz seems to have done so.

What happened at midnight is described three ways from one verb. Keil has him startled on waking, because he observed someone lying at his feet, and bending forward or to one side to feel who was there. Ellicott gives the same sense more briefly: the word means startled rather than afraid, the verb is literally to bend oneself, and he wakes with a start and in turning sees a woman at his feet. Wesley disposes of the hour in five words: he did not discover her sooner. Clarke reports instead how much trouble the verb gave the old paraphrast, who rendered it that the man trembled till his flesh became like a boiled turnip; and the same paraphrast added that Boaz subdued himself, comparing him to Joseph in Egypt and to the husband who set a sword between himself and Michal. Clarke draws from the verse the point that matters for the chapter's difficulty: it is fully evident that Boaz had no intimation whatever of what was in hand.
9:
Where the figure of the wing comes from divides them squarely. Clarke takes it from the birds: the wing is the emblem of protection, the metaphor drawn from the young of fowls which run under their mothers' wings to be saved from birds of prey, so that the sense is, take me to thee for wife. Keil denies exactly that: the expression is not taken from birds spreading their wings over their young, but refers to the corner of the counterpane, which a man spreads over his wife as well as himself. Ellicott holds both ends at once, giving the literal wing, reporting that the old paraphrast made the words in themselves a claim to espousal, and illustrating from the prophet who uses the image of marriage and from the gospel image of a bird gathering her brood. Clarke, though he argues for the birds, supplies the strongest evidence for the other side: to this day a Jew marrying throws the skirt of his talith over the bride to signify that he has taken her under his protection. Keil adds that the word stands as a dual but cannot be a pausal form where it sits, and is most probably a singular.

The praise Boaz gives is harder than it looks, and Clarke says so outright: it is not easy to find out what he means. His own solution is to take the word we translate kindness as piety, so that the later act proves her sincerity better than anything inferable from her having become a proselyte; and he draws the corollary that she did not seek the marriage to mend her condition, since she might have had a rich young man. Keil and Wesley agree on a plainer division: the earlier kindness was what she had shown to her dead husband and her mother-in-law, the later that, being a young widow, she did not go after young men as young women generally do, but turned to an older man so that her husband might have a successor. Ellicott reads the blessing for what it settles rather than what it means, noting that it follows immediately on her giving her name, and that the answer is itself sufficient proof both of the view Boaz took of her conduct and of the integrity of his own — he is prepared not merely to discharge the duty of next of kin but to do it in no perfunctory spirit. He also passes on two later readings, one that Ruth was given foreknowledge of the Messiah's birth through her line, and one from an early father comparing her to the Gentile church, the wild olive grafted in. Gill keeps to the manner of the reply: instead of calling her immodest for lying at his feet, or bold for asking marriage when she was poor, or being angry at being frightened out of sleep, he blesses her and calls her his daughter.

What she was told not to fear Gill alone spells out, and he finds three things in it — being forced and defiled, to which she had exposed herself; being reproached afterwards as an immodest woman; and being despised as poor and failing in her suit. The security offered is public: Keil has the whole city know her for a virtuous woman, and Ellicott notes that the word is literally the gate, the meeting-place of those going in and out. On the obstacle the two who touch it differ over the degree of kinship. Gill makes it close and simple, her husband and Boaz having been the sons of brothers and so cousins. Clarke supposes otherwise, that a brother of Elimelech was still living and so had the prior right, Boaz being only a nephew; and he adds that Naomi very likely knew nothing of it, which is why her plan had not allowed for it.
13:
Why she had to stay till morning is agreed. Gill says it was for her safety and honour and from no design upon her, and alone looks at the page besides, reporting that the first letter of the word for tarry is written larger than usual — a mark, some say, to fix attention on so singular a thing as a widow lodging with a man without any loss of chastity. Wesley reads the whole encounter through a summary he quotes entire from an earlier bishop: instead of touching her as a wanton, Boaz blessed her as a father, encouraged her as a friend, promised her as a kinsman, and sent her away laden with hopes and gifts, no less chaste but more happy than she came. Henry adds what the others leave out. She lay at his feet and not by his side, and went as soon as there was light, before one could know another; she was not ashamed to be known for a gleaner, but would not willingly be known abroad at night, her virtue being her greatest honour. On the charge of secrecy he is franker: though neither needed care much what was said while both were conscious of an unspotted purity, few could come so near the fire without being scorched, so that discovery would have raised suspicions in some and reflections from others — good people troubled, and bad people triumphant. He alone adds the practical reason, that if the matter took wind it might prejudice the other kinsman's freedom of choice.

Ellicott, at the same verse, quotes Henry by name for the rule of the thing, that we must keep not only a good conscience but a good name, and avoid not only sin but scandal; and he observes that the word is the woman, this woman, so that it is of Ruth and not of himself that Boaz is thinking.

The parting gift raises two questions. Clarke notes that the Hebrew names no quantity, and reasons from the paraphrast's own addition: rendering it six seahs, at two gallons and a half apiece, he felt the load too heavy for a woman, which is why he adds that she received strength from the Lord to carry it — where the smaller measure gives some four gallons, a goodly present and no miracle. Henry, reporting the same addition, thinks Boaz gave as much as she could well carry, the gift being evidence he had not sent her away in dislike; like a prudent corn-master he kept account of what he delivered out. Ellicott raises a harder point nobody else notices: the verb at the end of the verse is masculine in the current Hebrew, so it should read he went, and the old paraphrast marks this by supplying Boaz as subject — though many manuscripts, with the Syriac and Latin, take it as feminine, and the Greek cannot show the difference. On that reading Boaz goes to the city to find the nearer kinsman while Ruth goes home.

Naomi's question at the door is read three ways. Keil takes it as asking in what circumstances she comes, which really means what she has accomplished; Ellicott, that it can hardly be a question about her identity and means rather how she has fared; Wesley, that it is not doubt but wonder — art thou in very deed my daughter, and how camest thou hither so early? Keil notes that the expression about how the matter will fall rests on the image of a lot falling to the ground. Gill and Clarke agree on the counsel that closes the chapter: keep at home, say nothing of the affair, be easy about it until the issue is known — Clarke adding that Boaz lost no time in bringing it to one.
